bull.b: The high share of revenue from 7nm and more advanced nodes demonstrates sustained customer reliance on TSMC’s leading-edge manufacturing platform. This mix supports pricing power, technological relevance, and durable demand as AI, cloud, and high-performance computing expand.

Rapid revenue and earnings growth combined with exceptionally high margins indicate strong operating leverage and customer demand. This profitability gives TSMC resources to fund technology development, capacity expansion, and shareholder returns while preserving resilience through industry cycles.

bull.t: Conservative balance sheet and cash generation
bull.b: Declining leverage and operating cash flow above net income provide financial flexibility for a capital-intensive foundry model. A stronger equity base and high-quality cash generation help TSMC fund expansion internally and absorb fluctuations in semiconductor demand.

bear.b: The transition to N2 and the ramp of overseas facilities will temporarily raise costs before scale and yields mature. This creates a meaningful risk that strong revenue growth will not translate proportionally into earnings, while expansion costs may remain relevant across several quarters.

Packaging is an increasingly important part of delivering advanced chips, so constrained capacity can limit customers’ production even when wafer demand is strong. Until planned investments add sufficient capacity, this bottleneck may defer revenue and reduce the benefit of leading-edge demand.

bear.t: Heavy reinvestment and cash conversion pressure
bear.b: TSMC’s growth strategy requires very large investments in advanced nodes, overseas fabs, and packaging. Although these projects support long-term capacity, the spending reduces near-term free-cash-flow conversion and increases exposure to execution, utilization, and semiconductor-cycle risks.
